assignments.title: 1.1 VR Assignment — Create an Eisenhower Matrix in VR
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
1.1 VR Assignment — Create an Eisenhower Matrix in VR

Apply the principles of time management and goal setting to your current academic and personal tasks. This is Part 1 of a two-part workflow — you'll continue in Assignment 1: Time Management & Goal Setting.

Step 1: Create an Eisenhower Matrix in VR

  1. Upload the Eisenhower Matrix image (below) to your VR platform's file storage so you can spawn it in a VR session (in a space of your choosing).
  2. Start by writing down 10 to 20 of your current tasks, assignments, and responsibilities on sticky notes. Include everything — schoolwork, extracurricular activities, chores, and anything else you need to get done.
  3. Use the Eisenhower Matrix template to categorize your tasks. Place each task in the appropriate quadrant based on its urgency and importance.
    • Quadrant 1 (Top Right): Urgent and Important — Tasks to do immediately
    • Quadrant 2 (Top Left): Important but Not Urgent — Tasks to plan for
    • Quadrant 3 (Bottom Right): Urgent but Not Important — Tasks to delegate or do quickly
    • Quadrant 4 (Bottom Left): Not Urgent and Not Important — Tasks to eliminate or minimize
  4. Take a picture of your tasks scattered across the matrix.
  5. Prioritize your tasks. After placing your tasks in the matrix, go back to Quadrant 1 (those tasks that need your immediate attention). Rearrange these specific tasks in order of priority (the one you most need to get done quickly first, then the next, then the next).
  6. Take a close-up picture of the tasks in Quadrant 1 you put in priority order. These will be the focus of the next steps.

YOU'LL DO THE NEXT STEPS IN THE NEXT ASSIGNMENT. (See Assignment 1: Time Management & Goal Setting.)

Submit

Below submit BOTH:

  1. A picture of your overall matrix with all tasks across all quadrants.
  2. A close-up picture of the Quadrant 1 tasks placed in order of priority.

assignments.title: Assignment 1: Time Management & Goal Setting
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
Assignment 1: Time Management & Goal Setting

Apply the principles of time management and goal setting from Lesson 1 to your current academic and personal tasks. This assignment is the second half of a two-part workflow — Step 1 (the Eisenhower Matrix in VR) was completed in 1.1 VR Assignment.

Step 1: Create an Eisenhower Matrix in VR

YOU DID THIS IN THE LAST ASSIGNMENT. (See 1.1 VR Assignment.) The matrix and your prioritized Quadrant 1 tasks feed into Step 2 below.

Step 2: Create a SMART-Goal Breakdown

  1. Select a priority task. Choose one of the most important tasks from Quadrant 1 of your Eisenhower Matrix that has to deal with school (studying for a test, completing a project, something like that).
  2. Set a SMART goal. Break down your chosen task into a SMART goal. Remember, your goal should be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

Example:

  • Specific: I want to finish my history essay.
  • Measurable: The essay needs to be 1,500 words long.
  • Achievable: I will write 300 words each day for five days.
  • Relevant: This essay is worth 20% of my final grade in history.
  • Time-bound: I will complete the essay by next Wednesday at 8 PM.
  1. Break down the goal. Now, break your SMART goal into smaller, manageable tasks or milestones. For the example above, these might include researching the topic, writing the introduction, drafting each section, revising, and proofreading.

Step 3: Create a Schedule

  1. Use your SMART goal. Based on the breakdown you created in Step 2, plan out when you'll complete each task.
  2. Block out time. Use a weekly calendar or planner to block out specific times to work on your tasks. Be sure to include time for breaks, other assignments, and any extracurricular activities.
  3. Review and adjust. Check your schedule to ensure it's realistic. Make any necessary adjustments to fit everything in without overwhelming yourself.

Submit

Submit one Word document containing your priority task, your SMART goal (with all five letters marked), your task breakdown, and your schedule. Upload via the OneDrive tab on this assignment in Canvas.

File name: LastName_FirstName_TimeManagement_MJCRT

assignments.title: 1.2 VR Assignment — Build Your Own Mnemonic Device
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
1.2 VR Assignment — Build Your Own Mnemonic Device

The assignment, in two parts. First, some setup. Then the practice.

Part 1: Read this

Full Lesson — Harry Lorayne-Style Memory Tricks

Mnemonic devices have been helping people remember things for thousands of years. You've probably used them without even thinking about it. Remember "Never Eat Soggy Waffles" for the cardinal directions (North, East, South, West)? Or "Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally" for the order of math operations (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply, Divide, Add, Subtract)? These simple word tricks work because they turn boring lists into memorable phrases.

One man, Harry Lorayne, took this basic idea and developed an entire, powerful system for remembering all sorts of things. Instead of just using words, he created vivid mental movies — the sillier, the more outlandish, the more unique the better and easier it will be to remember. Here are his best tricks with real examples.

The Link System

Link items in a list through a crazy story. For example, to remember a shopping list of "milk, eggs, bread, apples," picture this: "A giant milk carton crying tears of eggs. As the eggs crash to the ground, instead of yolk, loaves of bread ooze out of shells. Then the bread slices grow apple trees from their crusts." Notice that the story doesn't make much sense, but the imagery is crazy! Once you picture that sequence in your mind you will almost never forget the details of that list.

Substitute Words

Similarly you can turn new or difficult words — or even names — into easy pictures. While learning the Spanish word for "to be in pain" — doler — perhaps you notice that doler sounds a lot like the English dollar. So picture a giant dollar bill hunched over holding its tummy, writhing in pain. For the name "George Rodriguez," you can first imagine a "gorge" (a deep crack in the ground) and then "Road-rig-ez" — picture a road with a big truck rig that says "EZ" on it.

Face-Name Memory

Suppose you just met George Rodriguez. How do you remember that that name goes with this guy? Connect his face to his name! Find the first thing about his face that jumps out at you and tie your substitute word example to that thing. Maybe George has a big gap between his teeth — that could be the gorge the big-rig truck is jumping over in your imagination. Boom! Every time you see George you'll picture this and you'll never forget his name.

Number Memory

This is one of the most powerful techniques: numbers. Turn numbers into pictures using the phonetic system. First, replace single digits with some consonant sound(s):

  • 0 = S, Z, or soft-C sound ("zzzzzero" starts with this sound)
  • 1 = T or D sound (1, t, and d all have one downward stroke)
  • 2 = N sound (n has two downward strokes)
  • 3 = M sound (m has three downward strokes)
  • 4 = R sound ("fourrrr" ends in this sound)
  • 5 = L sound (holding out five fingers forms an "L" with your index and thumb)
  • 6 = J, soft-G, or soft-CH (a 6 looks like an inverted lowercase "g")
  • 7 = K, hard-G, hard-C, or hard-CH sound (you can make a "K" out of 7s)
  • 8 = F or PH sound (an 8 looks like a lower-case cursive "f")
  • 9 = P, B, or V sound (a 9 looks like a backwards "P")
  • (Vowel sounds aren't used to represent numbers but will be used to help make words.)

Then make words out of the sounds that the numbers represent! The number 42 becomes "rain" (R-N). Remember your locker combination 15-23-8 by picturing a "tall enemy foe" (T-L = 15, N-M = 23, F = 8).

These tricks work because your brain remembers pictures better than words or numbers. Practice with small lists first, then work up to bigger challenges.

Visual lesson on the Lorayne mnemonic system (Canva embed).

Part 2: Do this

Go into VR and create a mnemonic device of your own using images, sticky notes, 3D objects, drawings, and/or sounds.

  1. Figure out something you need to remember. It could be some facts for science class, some vocab for a language class, a formula in math, the names and faces of historical figures, a list of important dates, even a sequence of controller-buttons to enable a cheat code in a video game.
  2. Go into VR and create a mnemonic device using images you upload to your VR platform's file storage, 3D drawings, sticky notes, or some props or sounds. Whatever you do, make sure it's relevant enough for you to remember what you need to remember and silly enough that you actually do.
  3. Save the mnemonic device as a snapshot for your own future reference.
  4. Save a recorded video of yourself explaining the mnemonic device you created. This is what you will submit below for credit.

Submit

Upload your video recording of yourself explaining your mnemonic device. Download the video from your VR platform and upload it here in Canvas.

Assignment 3: Critical Thinking, Research, and Presentation Skills

Here you are going to practice your researching, argumentative-writing, and presentation skills.

What to do

assignments.title: 1.4 VR Assignment — Inner Sanctum of Silence and Isolation
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
1.4 VR Assignment — Inner Sanctum of Silence and Isolation

Stress can be a killer. Sometimes we just need a quiet, isolated place to unwind.

Go into VR and create your own Inner Sanctum of Silence and Isolation, a place you can retreat to for quick breaks.

What to do

  1. Choose an environment that's appropriate to your goal.
  2. Choose a space in that environment that makes sense.
  3. Cultivate that space into a Sanctum — use props, images, 3D spheres, audio files, … whatever makes sense to you.
  4. Create a snapshot of your Inner Sanctum of Silence and Isolation.
  5. Upload that snapshot here (or if it's too personal, just take some pictures of parts of it as proof and share those).

Example: I used an "AI" generative image maker to make a 3D sphere (aka "a skybox") of a wizard's library in a medieval castle. Then I spawned that sphere image at the Medieval Castle environment, in one of the towers. I decked the space out with lit candles, dozens of old books, jars full of fairies and tiny dragons, bone dice, and other sorts of things you might find in a wizard's library. I added fire-burning sounds to torches (a subtle touch). I even included a secret portal that teleports me into the space (the trick is to "pull" a torch outside the castle wall like a secret passage entrance). That's my Inner Sanctum of Silence and Isolation.

Submit

A snapshot of your Inner Sanctum. If the whole space feels too personal to share, submit a few partial shots of pieces of it as proof you built it.

assignments.title: 2.1 VR Assignment — The Wordless Museum of Emotion & Intention
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
2.1 VR Assignment — The Wordless Museum of Emotion & Intention

Objective: See for yourself the power of the nonverbal aspects of communication.

Build five "scenes" or "emotion statues" in VR that communicate complex human experiences without using any written or spoken language. That means:

  • 🚫 No labels
  • 🚫 No audio explanations
  • 🚫 No symbols that contain language (e.g., "💔" is OK, but "📚" isn't if it clearly means "book" as a word)

Instead, use avatars, emoji props, poses, color, spacing, drawings, gestures (using Spatial MyRecs), object arrangements, and symbolism to make your meaning clear — or intriguingly unclear.

The 5 Prompts

1. Prompt: Show that someone is nervous.

  • Can be abstract or literal.
  • You can use gestures, spacing, posture, etc.

2. Prompt: Show that one person is disappointed with another person.

3. Prompt: Show that one person is disappointed with another for doing something she had promised she wouldn't do again.

  • Same emotion as Scene 2 — but this time add nuance and narrative.
  • How can you suggest backstory without words?

4. Prompt: Show that someone is saying goodbye, but secretly doesn't want to leave.

  • Use contrast: facial expression vs. body movement, direction vs. gesture.

5. Prompt: Create a scene that could be interpreted in more than one way.

  • For example, are these people angry? Full of joy?
  • Use this to explore how much context affects communication.
  • After building it, step back and ask: "What are the possible interpretations?"

Submit

  1. After setting up scenes for all of the 5 prompts, create a Video MyRec tour of the scenes. Tour slowly and thoroughly enough that someone who isn't you (namely, me) can see all the details and the big picture of each scene to really interpret the goings-on for himself.
  2. Write or record a one-paragraph reflection on the experience — what part of this was challenging? What part was easy? What lesson(s) did you learn about communication from this exercise?

Submit both the video tour file and the audio or written reflection below.

assignments.title: Assignment 1: Super Clear Instructions 🤖
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
Assignment 1: Super Clear Instructions 🤖

Goal: Learn to break a complex task into clear, manageable steps and represent it visually. You'll also assess and revise your instructions for clarity.

Step 1: Write Your Task Breakdown

  • Choose a single task (from a hobby, school project, or daily routine).
  • Write clear, step-by-step instructions as if for someone who's never done it.
  • Include necessary materials/tools and any common mistakes or tips.
  • Ensure logical flow between steps.

Step 2: Create a Flowchart

  • Make a visual representation of your task's steps.
  • Show any optional paths or decision points.
  • Use a tool of your choice (hand-drawn or digital).
  • Here is an example:

Step 3: Self-Assessment & Revision

  • Use the checklist below to review your breakdown and flowchart.
  • Revise to improve clarity, completeness, and flow.

Self-Assessment Checklist

Clarity

  • Are steps clear enough for a beginner?
  • Did I avoid unnecessary jargon?
  • Is each step concise but complete?

Logical Flow

  • Do steps follow a natural order?
  • Are all decisions and transitions explained?

Completeness

  • Are all tools/materials listed?
  • Are common errors or tips included?

Flowchart

  • Does it match the written breakdown?
  • Are steps clearly labeled?
  • Are branching paths shown, if needed?

Revision

  • Did I revise after completing the checklist?
  • Are my final instructions as clear as possible?

Submit

  1. Your revised task breakdown
  2. Your flowchart (PDF, image, or drawing)
  3. A short reflection (2–3 sentences) on what was most challenging and what you improved

Have fun!

assignments.title: 2.2 VR Assignment — The Clarity Challenge
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
2.2 VR Assignment — The Clarity Challenge

Objective: Practice adapting your communication style by explaining a single task at three different levels of detail.

Instructions

1. Choose a Task

  • Pick a real-world action that takes several steps to do:
  • Examples: tying shoes, brewing tea, unlocking a phone, logging into a website, folding a paper airplane.

2. Write 4 Explanations

Write four versions of your instructions:

  • 🔹 10 words or fewer
  • 🔹 25 words
  • 🔹 50 words
  • 🔹 As many words as you want

Each version should aim to be clear — but notice what gets easier or harder as you expand.

3. Build 4 Zones in VR

  • Create four labeled "explanation spaces" in your VR world.
  • Use signs, floating text, or voice recordings to share each version.
  • Arrange any props or objects to help demonstrate the task.

4. Reflect in VR (or in writing)

Add a fifth zone labeled "Reflection" or write your answers:

  • What got lost in the 10-word version?
  • What got clearer in the longer versions?
  • Which explanation was most effective for someone who doesn't know the task?

Submit

  • A Video MyRec walkthrough of your four explanations + reflection (recorded or live).
  • Or screenshots of each station plus your written reflection.

🔧 Optional Extension

Try explaining to a specific audience (a kid, a grandparent, or an alien). How would your wording change?

assignments.title: Assignment 2: Communication Style Analysis & Writing for Different Audiences
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
Assignment 2: Communication Style Analysis & Writing for Different Audiences

Objective: This assignment will help you recognize different communication styles and adapt your writing to suit various audiences. You will learn how communication that is too technical or too vague can lead to confusion and how adjusting the style of communication based on your audience can improve clarity and effectiveness.

Step 1: Communication Style Analysis

You will analyze two different communication styles: one that is overly technical and one that is too vague. Both examples will explain the same task but in very different ways. Your job is to compare and contrast the two styles, reflecting on how each style might cause challenges in task completion.

The examples are at the bottom of this page. The questions to consider for your analysis follow:

  • How does each style affect the clarity of the instructions?
  • What are the potential strengths or weaknesses of each style?
  • Which style is more likely to lead to confusion or misunderstandings?
  • How could the instructions be improved for clearer communication?

Submission: Write a short paragraph (about 150 words) discussing the pros and cons of both communication styles and explain which you think is more effective for task delegation.

Step 2: Writing for Different Audiences

You will now take the detailed task breakdown you created in the previous assignment in this module and rewrite it for two different audiences (you know, the assignment where I used making a PBJ sandwich as an example):

  1. A peer who may have some experience with a similar task.
  2. A younger sibling or someone who has no experience with the task and is unfamiliar with its complexity.

After writing the two versions, reflect on how you adapted the language, tone, and details for each audience. Consider:

  • What changes did you make in terms of vocabulary or complexity?
  • How did you adjust the level of detail?
  • Why were these changes necessary for the specific audience?

Submission: Submit both versions of the task breakdown, as well as a short reflection (100–150 words) on the differences between the two and why those changes were important.

Submission Requirements

  • Your analysis of the two example writing styles (below), with a short reflection.
  • Both rewritten versions of your Task Breakdown from the previous Soft Skills Assignment (for an experienced person and for a super inexperienced person), with a short reflection.

Example Paragraphs for Step 1

Highly Technical Style

To diagnose a non-starting vehicle where the accessories activate but the engine does not attempt to turn over, begin by testing the starter circuit. Using a multimeter, measure the voltage at the starter solenoid's control terminal while turning the key to the 'Start' position. A reading of 12V indicates the ignition switch and relay are functioning correctly. If no voltage is detected, inspect the starter relay and neutral safety switch for continuity. Additionally, verify that the battery maintains a minimum of 12.6V under load. If proper voltage reaches the solenoid but the starter does not engage, perform a voltage drop test across the starter motor's power and ground connections. Resistance above 0.2 ohms suggests excessive corrosion or a failing starter motor.

Highly Vague Style

If your car won't start but the lights and radio work, the problem is probably with the starter. First, double check the battery. Then may need to check a few things like fuses or wires, but if that doesn't help, you might have to replace the starter.

Any questions, let me know. Otherwise, have fun!

assignments.title: 2.3 VR Assignment — Fix the Miscommunication!
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
2.3 VR Assignment — Fix the Miscommunication!

Goal: Guided by using the Transactional Model of Communication, use VR to explore and fix a scenario where communication goes wrong.

🔧 Instructions

1. Build a Miscommunication Scene

Choose a real-life situation where communication fails. Examples:

  • A group project meeting where someone didn't understand the plan
  • A disagreement between two friends
  • A confusing job interview
  • A family dinner where someone misinterprets a joke
  • A game strategy session where a player misheard the plan
  • Different cultural meanings of the same word
  • One person assuming silence means agreement
  • People using different communication styles (direct vs. indirect)

In VR:

  • Set up avatars or labeled objects to show the people involved
  • Use props, drawings, or signs to show what's being said or felt
  • Include nonverbal cues: facial expressions, gestures, body language
  • Show where the communication broke down

2. Pause and Reflect

In your VR space, write or record your thoughts using a notepad, whiteboard, or sticky note wall. Answer:

  • What went wrong in this conversation?
  • What part of the Transactional Model was missing or misused?
  • How could this have gone better?

3. Rebuild the Scene with Better Communication

Make a new version of the same scene nearby that shows how the conversation could go right.

  • Adjust tone, gestures, or expressions
  • Add clarifying questions like "Wait — do you mean…?"
  • Include signs of active listening (nodding, pausing, responding)
  • Fix nonverbal or cultural misunderstandings

4. Record or Capture Your Scene

  • Record a Video MyRec tour explaining how your improved version shows better communication.
  • Or take screenshots comparing the "Before" and "After" versions and include a written explanation of how your improved version shows better communication.

5. Final Reflection

In your Video MyRec or on paper, answer:

  • What made the communication more successful in the second version?
  • Which changes made the biggest difference?

📤 Submit

Submit below either the Video MyRec tour of the multiple scenes along with your oral explanation and reflection, or pictures of the VR scenes and your written explanation and reflection.

Develop awareness of miscommunication and practice crafting clear and effective communication.

assignments.title: 2.4 VR Assignment — Creative Adaptation
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
2.4 VR Assignment — Creative Adaptation

Objective: Practice thinking on the fly when plans change.

Instructions

  1. Think of some simple event you'd enjoy being a part of (e.g. inviting friends over for a game night, going to your favorite sporting event, hanging out at the beach).
  2. Go into a VR session and start to create a representation of that event using IFX, drawings, images, sticky notes, audio files, whatever. Anticipate building for 15 to 20 minutes.
  3. BOOM! Disaster strikes. When you're what feels halfway through building that original scene (when you see about half of what you envisioned turned into reality OR you can set a timer for 10 minutes to flag the "disaster") STOP.
  4. Think of something that could've gone wrong during the actual event you're representing (playing off our previous examples: the power goes out so no one can play video games, one of the players during the sporting event just walks out mid-game, a rabid dog shows up at the beach). Feel free to ask an AI bot in ENGAGE or something like ChatGPT outside of it if you're struggling to come up with some event-altering event.
  5. In light of this change in the situation, think of a creative alternative to the original plan and finish your build in a way that represents this shift. (Again, continuing the previous examples, you might shift the event to tell scary stories, try to jump onto the field to take the player's position, try to capture the rabid dog in a trap made of umbrellas and beach towels, respectively.)
  6. Create a Video MyRec tour of your scene explaining the event before the disaster and then how you adjusted.
  7. Spend a few minutes reflecting on the exercise, and the power and benefit of being able to creatively adjust to altered plans on the fly.

2.5 VR Assignment — Decision Detective, Round 2

This time, you're going to go into VR to practice!

What to do

Step 1: Go into VR and write down on sticky notes at least TWO options of a real decision you're facing now.

Step 2: For each option, write down at least three possible outcomes on sticky notes. Clearly label each outcome's value using easy terms ("Good," "Okay," "Bad," recalling that multiple outcomes can have the same value rating). THEN REPRESENT THOSE OUTCOMES WITH IFX, IMAGES, DRAWINGS, SPATIAL MYRECS, ETC.

Step 3: For each outcome you listed, write down how likely it is (recalling again that multiple outcomes can be equally (un)likely):

  • Likely
  • Somewhat likely
  • Unlikely

Step 4: Finally, using the outcomes and likelihoods you've written down, clearly state your decision and explain on a Video MyRec exactly why you chose this option. Look for the outcome with the most high goods that are most likely; conversely, avoid the option that has the more likely bad things.

assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
2.6 VR Assignment — VR-Style "Reverse-Engineering Roadmap"

Objective: Use reverse-engineering to break down a personal goal into manageable steps, demonstrating planning, sequencing, and self-reflection.

Instructions

Okay, now that you've gotten some good practice thinking through the reverse-engineering process, we're taking this to the next level! Follow these easy steps:

  • Step 1: Choose a new goal you're excited about — academic, personal, or extracurricular.
  • Step 2: Go into a session in VR, and choose a location with a mountain, temple, pyramid, or some other clearly ascending, sloped structure.
  • Step 3: Go to the top of a mountain (or pyramid or whatever) and using some combination of IFX, images, drawings, sticky notes, Spatial MyRecs, and audio clips create a scene representing you achieving your goal. Make the scene come alive — the goal here is to inspire yourself to greatness.
  • Step 4: Step down a level / back a few paces and in a briefer form represent the action item you have to take just before reaching your goal. Then step down another level and represent (briefly) the action you have to take just before that one, then go down a bit further and represent that action you have to take just before that one, and on and on till you've represented all the steps of your plan starting from TODAY.
  • Step 5: Starting at the bottom of your action plan, start a Video MyRec and both show and explain each action step from the very first step all the way up the mountain (pyramid, whatever) to the final scene that shows you achieving your goal.
  • Reflection: Conclude with a brief reflection explaining how reverse-engineering your goal makes it feel easier and clearer to achieve. Note in particular anything that you were surprised by during the reverse-engineering thinking process, and also how inspiring it is (if it is) to see the scene of your goal achieved at the very top.

This exercise will help you take control of your dreams, providing a practical method to make them come true!

assignments.title: 2.7 VR Assignment — The Fact-Opinion Museum Curation Challenge
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
2.7 VR Assignment — The Fact-Opinion Museum Curation Challenge

Objective: Construct, label, and reflect on a virtual museum exhibit that challenges the traditional fact-opinion distinction by analyzing statements, categorizing them, and defending your classifications — showing the two dimensions: truth and belief.

Instructions

  1. Create a 3D "Museum of Statements":
    • Create notes of 12 statements (these can be sticky notes, written with 3D pen, or written on a whiteboard).
    • Example statements to include (but you can come up with your own too):
      1. "Ducks are good swimmers."
      2. "Murder is wrong."
      3. "Water is H₂O."
      4. "I like cheese."
      5. "Pineapple on pizza is gross."
      6. "George Washington was the first president."
      7. "Studying helps you succeed in school."
      8. "Slavery is wrong."
      9. "Video games rot your brain."
      10. "Beauty is objective."
      11. "AI will destroy humanity."
      12. COME UP WITH YOUR OWN TWELFTH STATEMENT.
  2. Create Two Axes in the Museum:
    • Axis 1: Truth Value (True ↔ False)
    • Axis 2: Belief Confidence (Strongly Believe ↔ Unsure)
    • Place each statement in the VR museum space according to where it fits on these two axes.
    • Tag each statement you place with a third label: Substantive vs. Mere Opinion
  3. Record a Short Video or Audio Tour (3–5 mins):
    • Make a Video MyRec of you walking through your museum exhibit.
    • Explain your reasoning for why each statement is placed where it is.
    • Reflect on at least ONE example where a "mere opinion" might actually become "substantive" with reasoning.
    • End the tour by challenging the viewer: "What do you think? Would you move anything?"

assignments.title: 2.8 VR Assignment — The Danger Zone: When "It's Just My Opinion" Goes Wrong
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
2.8 VR Assignment — The Danger Zone: When "It's Just My Opinion" Goes Wrong

Objective: Highlight the practical danger of treating all value claims as equal.

Instructions

  1. Go into VR.
  2. Create a scenario using some combination of 3D objects, images, drawings, sticky notes, recorded walkthroughs, and audio clips to show a bad moral situation (keep it SFW, obviously). That is, show a situation where someone is doing something bad.
  3. Now suppose that that someone doing something bad uses "It's just your opinion that this is bad" to defend doing that thing that is morally troubling.
  4. Escalate the scene — show what happens when no one can challenge that behavior. How bad can things really get? Really think through the implications and the upshots of not being able to tell someone, "No! You're wrong. Don't do that!"
  5. Record a video of yourself explaining the initial scene and also explaining the escalated scene.
  6. Finally, wrap up your video offering your own moral reasons to push back.

assignments.title: Assignment 8: Reflecting on Moral Claims
assignments.html:
M/J CRITICAL THINKING
Assignment 8: Reflecting on Moral Claims

Objective: Moral claims (claims about right or wrong, good or bad, beauty or ugliness, etc.) are meaningful and often guide our most important decisions. This exercise is a chance to practice thinking critically about why these claims matter and how we can approach them thoughtfully.

Instructions

  1. Write a short reflection (150 words) answering the following questions:
    • Why do you think people often find it easier to dismiss evaluative claims (like "stealing is wrong" or "this painting is beautiful") as mere opinions?
    • How might avoiding the evaluation of such claims protect us from difficult conversations or decisions?
    • Can you think of a situation where treating an evaluative claim as "just an opinion" might have led to a bad outcome?
  2. Explain (100–150 words) how someone might evaluate a moral claim for its truthfulness. For example:
    • What types of evidence or reasoning could support or undermine a claim like "bullying is wrong" or "helping others is good"?
    • How could we decide whether one evaluative claim is better supported than another?

quizzes.title: Module 1 Intro — Preparing like an Intellectual
quizzes.description:
Before you start the module, answer these questions. Your responses help your teacher understand where the class is starting from.

About this module: An alternative title for this module might be "Academic Excellence." You'll cover time management and goal setting (Lesson 1), active reading, notetaking, and memory (Lesson 2), critical thinking, research, and presenting (Lesson 3), and collaborative learning, stress management, and test prep (Lesson 4). Each lesson has a paired written assignment and a paired VR assignment.

questions.text:
Essential Question · your first answer

What habits and skills make the difference between students who genuinely learn and students who just get through?

Module objectives · where do you need work?

Looking at the four lesson topics below, which one or two areas do you most need to improve? Pick all that apply.

answers.text: Active reading, memory techniques, and note-taking (Lesson 2)
Critical thinking, research, and presentation skills (Lesson 3)
Collaborative learning, stress management, and test prep (Lesson 4)

questions.text:
Confidence baseline

Right now, before doing any of this module's work, how confident do you feel about your ability to study and learn well on your own?

Group work opt-in

Would you like to be assigned a study group for the substantive assignment in this module? Group members complete one shared submission with the same rubric as solo students.

quizzes.description:
Before you start the module, answer these questions. Your responses help your teacher understand where the class is starting from.

About this module: In Module 1 you learned the practical, tangible skills for succeeding in school. Module 2 is about the harder kind of intellectual work — the kind that happens between people, and the kind that happens when smart people disagree. The first six lessons cover soft skills: giving clear instructions, recognizing communication styles, recovering from miscommunication, adapting, navigating cultural differences, and planning thoughtful action. The last two lessons cover normativity: distinguishing facts from opinions (and questioning whether that distinction even holds), and reasoning carefully about moral claims.
